prompt.context: Our client is a large national healthcare payer (health insurance company, think Aetna) exploring the launch of a new disease management ('DM') program to better serve its 5 million members. The idea is to hire and train a team of 'Health Coaches' to manage a portfolio of patients to reduce the costs of overall health expenditures (e.g. reminders to take drugs, provide limited medical advice, suggested diet, exercise etc). Studies show that once-a-month contact with each patient reduces health spending by 5% on average.
prompt.question: Should our client launch the program? If so, what steps should it take?

clarifying_info.q: What is happening in the broader industry?
clarifying_info.a: The whole industry is under pressure to innovate new products that will control spending.

clarifying_info.q: Are any competitors already doing this?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the client is first to market.

clarifying_info.q: Has automation been tried for disease management?
clarifying_info.a: Past attempts to purely automate DM have yielded minimal savings.

clarifying_info.q: How do Health Coaches work operationally?
clarifying_info.a: All activity is conducted remotely via phone/email, typically by a nurse that wants to work from home.

clarifying_info.q: How many patients can a Health Coach contact?
clarifying_info.a: It is difficult to actually reach patients, so Coaches can contact 8 members per day (assume 25 days per month).

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs of the program?
clarifying_info.a: Annual costs per Coach: $60K salary + 20% other (training, benefits, laptop, etc.). There are no other program costs.

exhibits.title: Client's member segmentation by disease type
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart breaking the client's 5 million members into three segments (Individual 15%, Group 65%, 65+ 20%) and within each segment further divided into disease categories: Healthy, Lifestyle, Hereditary, Degenerative, and Other.

disease_breakdown_within_segment.note: Exact disease-type percentages must be read from the chart; Lifestyle is the largest disease category across all segments.

exhibits.title: Average cost data (PMPM)
exhibits.shows: A table showing average cost Per Member Per Month (PMPM) across three member segments (Individual, Group, 65+) and three disease types (Lifestyle, Hereditary, Degenerative).

framework: Program Savings: quantify savings by customer segment and disease area; focus on cost per member and 5% reduction assumption
Program Costs: Health Coach salary ($60K base + 20% overhead = $72K/year), training, communication systems
Risks: accuracy of assumptions (5% savings rate, portfolio capacity), competitive response, regulatory and liability considerations

questions.prompt: Which customer segment and disease area should the client focus on first, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit A to identify the highest-cost, highest-benefit segment. The 65+ segment has the highest medical costs and 20% of members. Within 65+, Lifestyle diseases are the largest disease category and most amenable to behavior-change coaching. Strong answer: 65+ Lifestyle first because sicker patients drive higher costs, providing the greatest potential DM savings, and lifestyle diseases are behavior-driven so coaching is most impactful. Number of 65+ lifestyle members = 20% x 40% x 5,000,000 = 400,000.

math.setup: Number of 65+ lifestyle members = total members x 65+ segment share x lifestyle disease share
steps: 5,000,000 total members x 20% (65+ segment) = 1,000,000 members in 65+
math.answer: 400,000 members in the 65+ Lifestyle target segment

questions.prompt: Calculate the profitability of the Health Coach program for the 65+ Lifestyle segment.
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute cost per coach, portfolio size, savings per portfolio, and scale to the full coach team. Strong answer works through all unit conversions cleanly and arrives at ~$72K net profit per coach (2x return). Key insight: profit doubles the cost of each coach.

math.setup: Cost per Coach, Portfolio size, Savings per portfolio per year, then net profit
steps: Portfolio size = 8 patients/day x 25 days/month = 200 patients/coach
Annual savings per coach portfolio = $1,200 PMPM x 12 months x 5% savings x 200 patients = $144,000
Net profit per coach = $144,000 savings - $72,000 cost = $72,000
Number of coaches needed for 400,000 patients = 400,000 / 200 = 2,000 coaches
Total program profit = $72,000 net profit per coach x 2,000 coaches = $144,000,000/year
math.answer: $144 million annual profit; net profit per coach is $72K (a 2x return on coach cost)

questions.prompt: How does profitability look for the Individual and Group lifestyle segments?
questions.guidance: Using Exhibit B PMPM for Individual ($600) and Group ($400) versus 65+ ($1,200): Individual segment savings are 50% of 65+ savings, making it roughly break-even. Group segment savings are even lower ($400/$1,200 = 33% of 65+), making it a loss. Candidate should recognize that lower-cost members generate insufficient savings to cover the $72K coach cost.

math.setup: Same formula as Part 3 but substituting lower PMPM values
steps: Individual Lifestyle PMPM = $600; savings per patient/year = $600 x 12 x 5% = $360; savings per portfolio = $360 x 200 = $72,000; net = $72K - $72K = $0 (break-even)
Group Lifestyle PMPM = $400; savings per patient/year = $400 x 12 x 5% = $240; savings per portfolio = $240 x 200 = $48,000; net = $48K - $72K = -$24,000 (loss)
math.answer: Individual segment is break-even; Group segment is unprofitable at -$24K per coach

brainstorming.prompt: There are 650,000 Group members with lifestyle diseases left uncoached and the segment is currently unprofitable. What ideas would you suggest to make the Group segment (or the overall program) more profitable?

categories.name: More efficient DM program
ideas: Coaching at work (reach patients during work hours to improve contact rate)
Bi-monthly contact instead of monthly to reduce coach time per patient
Automated correspondence (email/app nudges) to supplement or replace some calls
Better training for Health Coaches to increase savings rate above 5%

categories.name: Seek additional revenue sources
ideas: Charge employers a fee to enroll their Group employees in the coaching service
Pursue government support as a state-approved or sponsored public-health program
Sell the Health Coach service to other payers (external commercialization)

categories.name: Client selection
ideas: Target members who are predicted to respond with savings well above the 5% average
Use data analytics to identify high-risk members with highest potential cost reduction

recommendation: The client should launch the Health Coaching program, beginning with a focused pilot on the 65+ Lifestyle disease segment
The program generates $72K net profit per coach (a 2x return) and $144M annually at full scale for the 65+ Lifestyle cohort
Expand to the Individual Lifestyle segment even at break-even, given customer retention and moral/brand rationale
Do not launch for the Group Lifestyle segment unless program efficiency improvements or additional revenue sources make it profitable
risks: The 5% cost-reduction assumption may not hold in practice; a pilot is needed to validate
Coach capacity assumption (8 contacts/day, 200 patients) may be overstated given difficulty reaching patients
Regulatory and liability risks of nurses providing remote medical-adjacent advice
Competitive response once others see the client's first-mover advantage erode
next_steps: Launch a controlled pilot program to validate key assumptions (5% savings rate, coach portfolio size, cost structure)
If pilot confirms economics, scale to all 400,000 members in the 65+ Lifestyle segment
Evaluate whether to offer the program to other payers as an external revenue stream
Analyze whether operational changes (automation, employer fees) can make the Group segment profitable
